name: Tea gardens
tagline: Sleep, walk and taste where the leaf grows
summary: Darjeeling's estates on the slopes between 600 and 2,000 m, Temi in South Sikkim and the low-country gardens of the Dooars. We plan factory visits in the plucking season, tastings by flush and nights in estate bungalows or homestays on the garden.
intro: Tea came to these hills as an experiment in the 1840s, when Archibald Campbell, the first superintendent of Darjeeling, planted China seeds at his house. Within thirty years the slopes held dozens of commercial estates, and the name Darjeeling became a geographical indication protected in law in 2004.

The year has a rhythm you can plan around. First flush is picked from about March to April, second flush in May and June, the monsoon flush through the rains and the autumn flush in October and November. Factories are busiest, and most worth seeing, in the plucking months. Most estates close their factory to visitors on Sundays and during winter dormancy: check current status before you travel.

name: Toy train
tagline: The 2-foot line from the plains to Ghum
summary: The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway, opened in 1881 and listed by UNESCO in 1999, climbs from New Jalpaiguri to Darjeeling on a 610 mm gauge with loops and reversing zig-zags. We book the steam and diesel joy rides, the full run when it operates, and plan the days around it.
intro: The line runs about 88 km from New Jalpaiguri to Darjeeling and rises to 2,258 m at Ghum, once the highest railway station in India. Its engineers used loops, where the track spirals over itself, and zig-zag reverses to gain height on slopes too steep for an ordinary railway.

Most visitors ride the short joy ride between Darjeeling and Ghum, which stops at the Batasia Loop. The through train from NJP takes most of a day, and landslides in the monsoon often cut the lower section. Seats are booked through Indian Railways, and timetables change by season: check current status before you travel.

name: Monasteries and dzongs
tagline: Prayer halls, chortens and fortress monasteries
summary: Ghum's Yiga Choeling, Rumtek and Enchey in Gangtok, Pemayangtse and Tashiding in West Sikkim, Zang Dhok Palri in Kalimpong and the great dzongs of Bhutan. We time visits to prayer hours and festival masks, and brief you on how to behave inside.
intro: Buddhism reached Sikkim in the 17th century with three lamas who met at Yuksom and crowned the first Chogyal in 1642. Bhutan was unified by the Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal from 1616, who built the dzongs that still serve as both monastery and seat of district government.

Visiting is free at most monasteries, though some charge a small entry or camera fee. Walk clockwise around chortens and prayer wheels, cover shoulders and knees, and ask before photographing monks or the inside of a lhakhang. In Bhutan's dzongs, Bhutanese visitors wear national dress and foreigners should dress formally.

name: Kangchenjunga views
tagline: Clear mornings on the third-highest peak
summary: Tiger Hill, Sandakphu, Pelling, Rinchenpong, Lava and the Chele La in Bhutan. Clear views of Kangchenjunga (8,586 m) are most likely from October to December and on dry mornings in spring, so we plan viewpoint nights in those months and leave a spare morning.
intro: Kangchenjunga is the third-highest mountain in the world and the guardian deity of Sikkim. From Darjeeling it fills the northern sky at about 75 km. From Sandakphu, on the Singalila ridge, four of the five highest peaks on earth are in sight on a clear day: Everest, Kangchenjunga, Lhotse and Makalu.

The catch is cloud. From June to September the mountains are hidden on most days. The best odds are from mid-October to December, when the air after the monsoon is dry, and again in February and March. Views come early: be at the viewpoint before sunrise and expect cloud by mid-morning.

name: High passes and lakes
tagline: Nathu La, Gurudongmar and the Silk Route
summary: Tsomgo Lake at 3,750 m, Nathu La on the China border, Gurudongmar at about 5,430 m and the Zuluk loops on the old trade road to Tibet. Permits, acclimatisation days and honest altitude advice are built into every route.
intro: The roads north and east of Gangtok climb from 1,650 m to above 4,000 m in a single morning. That speed is the risk. Altitude sickness can affect anyone above 2,500 m, and the plan should give the body time: a night at Lachen before Gurudongmar, for example, rather than a day trip from Gangtok.

Most of these places are in restricted or protected areas. Indian nationals need permits arranged through registered operators, foreign nationals cannot visit some of them at all, and roads close for snow and landslides. Check current status before you travel.

name: Jungle safaris
tagline: Rhino, gaur and elephant in the Dooars
summary: Jaldapara and Gorumara for the one-horned rhinoceros, Chapramari and Buxa for elephant and gaur, and Neora Valley for the red panda. Parks close in the monsoon, roughly mid-June to mid-September, so we plan safaris from October to May and book zones early.
intro: The Dooars hold the largest rhinoceros population in West Bengal, most of it in Jaldapara, with a smaller herd in Gorumara. Elephants move through the tea gardens and forests along old corridors between Nepal and Assam, and the gaur, the largest wild cattle in the world, is common.

Safaris are jeep drives and watchtower sessions run by the forest department, booked online in advance. Slots are limited at weekends and in the Puja holidays. The parks close for breeding in the monsoon: check current status before you travel.

name: Treks and walks
tagline: From village trails to the Goecha La
summary: Sandakphu–Phalut on the Singalila ridge, Goecha La from Yuksom, the Barsey rhododendron walk, Bhutan's Druk Path and easy tea-garden and village trails. Graded by hours, height gained and terrain, with local guides and porters.
intro: You do not need to be a mountaineer to walk here. Many of the best days are half-day trails between villages, through tea gardens or up to a monastery, with a car to meet you at the end. The longer treks, Sandakphu and Goecha La, need a few days of fitness work beforehand.

Trekking in Singalila National Park and in Kangchenjunga National Park needs permits and, in most cases, a registered guide. Spring (April–May) brings rhododendrons and autumn (October–November) brings clear views. Check current status before you travel.

name: Village homestays
tagline: Sleep in family homes, eat from the farm
summary: Homestays in Sittong, Lepchajagat, Sillery Gaon, Icchey Gaon, Dzongu, Uttarey, Hee Bermiok and the Bhutanese farmhouses of Paro and Haa. Simple rooms, home cooking and money that stays in the village, at a fraction of hotel prices.
intro: Homestays are the fastest-growing kind of stay in these hills and often the best value. A family lets two to six rooms, cooks for guests and knows the trails. Prices usually include all meals.

Expect clean but simple rooms, shared tables, hot water by geyser or bucket, and patchy mobile signal. We choose homestays where the family runs the place, not a city operator, and tell you plainly what the bathroom is like.

name: Honeymoons
tagline: Fewer moves, better rooms, a view each morning
summary: A heritage room in Darjeeling, a Pelling room facing Kangchenjunga, snow in Lachung, a slow Bhutan valley. We keep moves to a minimum, put the money where it counts (the room with the view) and save on the rest.
intro: A good hill honeymoon moves less than a sightseeing tour. We plan three bases at most in a week, two nights as the minimum anywhere, and one place where nothing is scheduled.

Spend where it shows: the room facing the mountains, a private car on the long drive days, one dinner somewhere special. Save on the rest. Snow is likeliest in Lachung, Zuluk and Tsomgo from December to March, if that is the picture you want.

name: Family trips
tagline: Short drives, warm rooms, no surprises
summary: Routes with drive days under five hours, family rooms, a toy-train ride, the zoo and mountaineering institute in Darjeeling, a jeep safari in the Dooars. We plan for ages and altitude, and say which places suit small children and grandparents.
intro: Hill roads are slow: 70 km can take three hours. Families travel better with fewer hotel changes, a mid-day stop and drives timed for after breakfast. We cap most transfer days at four or five hours.

Altitude matters with children and older travellers. Gangtok, Darjeeling and Pelling are fine for almost everyone; Tsomgo, Nathu La and Gurudongmar are not ideal for infants or anyone with heart or lung conditions. We tell you before you book.

name: Food and markets
tagline: Momo, thukpa, churpi and first-flush tea
summary: The haats and markets of the hills, Tibetan and Nepali kitchens, Lepcha and Bhutia home food, Bhutan's ema datshi and red rice, Dooars fish curries, and the old bakeries and tea rooms of Darjeeling and Kalimpong. Cheap to eat well, if you know where.
intro: Hill food is built for cold mornings and long days: noodle soups, dumplings, fermented greens (gundruk), fermented soybean (kinema), hard yak or cow cheese (churpi) and sel roti, a ring-shaped rice bread made for festivals.

Weekly haats are the best markets to see, and the cheapest places to eat are the small momo and thukpa shops near the bazaars. In Bhutan almost every dish has chilli as a vegetable rather than a spice: ask for it mild.

name: Festivals
tagline: Losar, tshechus, Dashain and Pang Lhabsol
summary: Masked dances at Bhutan's tshechus, Losar in the monasteries, Pang Lhabsol at Ravangla, Bumchu at Tashiding and Dashain and Tihar across the Gorkha hills. Most follow the lunar calendar, so we confirm dates each year before we build the route.
intro: The festival calendar here is lunar and Tibetan, so dates move by several weeks from one year to the next. Bhutan publishes its tshechu dates in advance; monastery festivals in Sikkim are announced closer to the time.
Festivals fill rooms. For Paro and Thimphu tshechus, the October Puja holidays and the Dashain fortnight, book stays two to three months ahead. Check current status before you travel.

name: Budget trips
tagline: Good trips that cost less, done properly
summary: Shared jeeps instead of reserved cars, homestays and tourist lodges instead of resorts, shoulder months instead of the Puja rush, and free viewpoints, walks and monasteries. Our budget plans keep the safety and the good bits and cut the rest.
intro: The cheapest way up from Siliguri is a shared jeep, usually a Bolero or Sumo with ten or eleven seats, for a few hundred rupees a seat. A reserved car on the same road costs a few thousand. Shared jeeps leave when they fill, from fixed stands near NJP and the Siliguri bus terminus.

The biggest savings are in timing. Hotel rates in the hills can halve between the peak weeks (April–June, the October Puja holidays, Christmas and New Year) and the quieter months. Monasteries, most viewpoints and many walks are free. Our budget packages say exactly what is included and what is not.

name: Birds and orchids
summary: Lava and Neora Valley, Latpanchar and Mahananda, Buxa, Kitam, Shingba's rhododendrons and the orchid nurseries of Kalimpong. Spring, from March to May, brings flowers and breeding birds; winter brings migrants to the rivers and forests of the foothills.
intro: The eastern Himalaya is one of the richest bird regions in Asia because the altitude changes so fast: tropical forest in the Dooars, temperate oak and rhododendron at 2,000 m and alpine meadows above 3,500 m, all within a day's drive.

Sikkim alone records more than 500 species of orchid, and Kalimpong's nurseries have grown and exported orchids and cacti for generations. Birding is best at first light; hire a local bird guide, who will know where the hornbills are feeding this week.
